newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Give Hong Kong a chance, urges legislator.
newsitem.headline: Give Hong Kong a chance, urges legislator.

text.p: Her businessman father fled from the communists in China, but Hong Kong politician Rita Fan has no plans to follow suit.

"To be fair to ourselves we should give ourselves a chance and stay put and see what happens," said Fan, chosen last month to be president of the legislature due to take over when the British colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30.

"I personally am very confident and convinced that we will have our lifestyle and our freedom as we have enjoyed all these years...the best way is to taste the pudding, and I think you'll like it," Fan said in an interview on Wednesday.
Fan was four years old when her family sought refuge in the British colony after the communist takeover of China in 1949.
Her Shanghai businessman father had no place in the anti-capitalist regime, she said, speaking at her tiny office in Hong Kong's Central business district.
But Fan said she had every confidence in Beijing's promise to treat Hong Kong differently under a one-country, two-systems formula that pledges considerable autonomy.
Beijing has promised to permit the free-wheeling way of life of the bustling trade entrepot continue unabated and not to impose communism on capitalist Hong Kong.
Not everyone in Hong Kong shares Fan's breezy confidence.
Hundreds of thousands have emigrated since Britain and China struck a treaty in 1984 governing Hong Kong's return.
She and her family have not obtained foreign passports.
Fan, a no-nonsense, straight-talking woman, blamed Britain and its "public" way of addressing issues over Hong Kong for the bumpy ride during the countdown.
That made Beijing defensive, she said, and resulted in the chill in Sino-British relations. Hong Kong's Chinese would not make the same mistake.

The Rita Fan of the 1980s was a staunch member of the colonial establishment she now criticises. She was appointed in 1983 by the British colonial governor to the then all-appointed Legislative Council, serving for nine years.
In the final three years, she also served as an Executive Councillor, a member of the Governor's circle of advisers.
"I was appointed by the British governor of Hong Kong to serve...and to serve is not to serve the British governor but to serve the people of Hong Kong," she said.

Fan joined Beijing's Preliminary Working Committee in July 1993, formulated to advise China on the handover, and graduated last year to the influential Preparatory Committee charged with forming Hong Kong's post-1997 administration.

Last month she was crowned president of the controversial Provisional Legislature that China plans to install in place of the current elected Legislative Council, undoing British-sponsored democratic reforms in Hong Kong that angered China.

Hong Kong's Democrats in particular have led the vocal attacks on the provisional legislature, arguing it has no legal right to exist and that it marks the first step towards the curtailing of Hong Kong's freedoms.

Fan insists the installation of the Provisional Legislature, along with plans to roll back some civil liberties laws on the grounds they violate the Basic Law, does not mean Hong Kong's freedoms will be snuffed out.
The Basic Law, Hong Kong's future constitution, was promulgated in 1990.

"What is promised to the Hong Kong people in the Basic Law in terms of democracy is more democratic than anything the British government has given us over the past 150 years of colonial rule," she said.
